content.content:
Opening a draft fixes a base. When `deccy draft <node>...` opens a draft for a node, the record written for that draft carries, beside its key, its three references and its state, a content-identity base of that node's owned set: an entry for every path the set holds at that moment — the node document, plus the repo-relative paths the node's `content.ref` lists when `ref` is an array, and the node document alone when it is inline (xzxtxymq) — giving the identity of the content that path holds, as that content is read from the change that owns it (nqktpzuu). The base is a value per path, determined by that path's content and by nothing else: equal content gives an equal entry, different content gives a different one. It is not a change id, an edit, a workspace, a path name, the tree of a change, the list of a change's paths, or metadata about any of them; an entry names no change, although the content it describes was read from one. It is a value and not a copy, so the record describes the content of the owned paths without becoming a second copy of it, and the registry carries no repository file as state (twpvqstu). The base is written into the draft's record and nowhere else: one JSON document at `.deccy/work/<handle>.json`, named by the handle the opening minted, the base a field of that one document, with no second file, no index beside the documents, and no marker in the draft's workspace, in a change or in a node document carrying any part of it. Reading it back is reading that document, because the documents are what the registry holds and there is nothing beside them to consult (twpvqstu).

Opening is the moment the base is taken, and the only moment. A draft's record first exists when the opening writes it: the opening writes each record `open` for the draft it was minted for, reports the handle and the workspace path, and creates the workspace the draft is written in; the base is taken as part of writing that first record and not as a later step that consults it again (szvotxpq). One draft, one record, one base: the record is minted for its draft, so the base belongs to that draft and to no other, and another record naming the same node — a competing draft or a redraft — carries its own base and never inherits this one (szvotxpq, owyntkvw). A base taken at any later moment would describe content the caller never saw: the draft's edits are made in its workspace against the owned content as it stood when that workspace and its record were made, so the moment of opening is the moment the base describes. Taking it reads the owned content and writes only the record, so the opening still touches no graph state: it creates no node, writes no `nodes/` document, draws no edge, moves no record's state, and leaves the graph a caller reads before the call and after it the same; the base changes none of that, being content the record carries in the untracked registry rather than anything attributed to a change (szvotxpq, twpvqstu, owyntkvw).

The base is carried content, not identity, and not a fourth reference. The record's identity remains the handle alone — minted for the draft, written into the record as its key, the one value that picks a record out — and the node, the edit and the workspace remain its three references, naming the parts of a draft rather than the record (owyntkvw). The base displaces none of them, re-keys none of them and re-labels none of them. It is not a key, because a base picks nothing out: two records may carry equal bases and remain two records, and an entry names no node, no edit and no workspace, so it cannot stand where the handle stands. It is not a reference either, and this decision does not make it one: a reference names a part of a draft, and the base names none; what it records is content, by a value derived from that content, which is why the three references stay exactly three. It is the other kind of field a record carries, the kind its state is: the opening writes `open`, a value that is neither the key nor a reference to any part of a draft, and the base is carried beside it in the same document (szvotxpq). The clause that makes the handle the whole of the record's identity and everything else it carries a reference does not close the record's field set, because its subject is which carried field could be the record's identity and its answer is the handle alone; that same settlement defers the record's base content, with its state and its lifetime, to the commitment that decides it, and this decision is that commitment cashed (owyntkvw). Nothing here makes the base the record's identity, and nothing here makes it a fourth reference: the handle stays the key, the three references stay three, the base is a value the record carries and reads back, and the path a record has is still `.deccy/work/<handle>.json` under the handle alone (owyntkvw, twpvqstu).

A draft is stale when its base no longer matches the owned set. The comparison is made at the landing — the recording of a draft's named edits into its node's change, `record <path>... --to <id>`, where `--to` names the one node whose change receives them — and it compares, path by path, the base the record carries with the content the owned set holds at that moment (rvyrosmp). The owned set is read as it stands then: the node document, and the repo-relative paths the node's `content.ref` lists then when `ref` is an array, or the node document alone when it is inline, and nothing else — the working copy's tree, the change's other paths and every path no ref of the node names are outside the comparison, so drift there neither makes a draft stale nor is named in a refusal, while a path the node has since added to its refs is a path the base does not hold and a path it has since dropped is a base entry the owned set no longer holds (xzxtxymq). Both sides are read from jj at the change that owns the node, under the caller-supplied binary and root, and not from the draft's working copy: the read that fixes a node document at its own change fixes what the base describes and what it is compared against, so a workspace whose files are absent, stale or newer than the change contributes nothing to either side, and a draft's own unrecorded edits in its workspace are not a difference at all, because the workspace is not the change that owns the content (nqktpzuu). The ref paths of that change are read by the same read at the same owning change, since it is the change that owns them (xzxtxymq). A path whose entry and whose content no longer agree, a path the base holds that the owned set has lost, and a path the owned set holds that the base does not are each a difference; the differences taken together are what makes the draft stale, and they are the differing paths.

A stale draft refuses landing, and it names the differing paths. When the recording is made and a record naming that node — one the opening wrote, whose draft has not landed — is stale, the recording is refused: it names that record's handle and, for that record, the differing paths of the owned set, and it lands nothing. No named edit is placed into any change, no node is created, no record's state is moved, and nothing of the graph is written (rvyrosmp, szvotxpq). The refusal is the precondition of the recording, not a second verb and not a second landing: `record` remains placement-only, `--to` still names the one change the edits would have entered, and a recording that does not place is a recording refused rather than a recording that places somewhere else (rvyrosmp). The paths it names are paths of the owned set of the node `--to` names, and they may be paths the call did not name: the base is a base of the whole owned set, and a node's document and its refs stand together, so recording one named path into a change whose owned content has moved would place an edit made against content the node no longer owns. When several records name the node, the rule holds for each of them — a recording is refused if any record naming that node is stale, and the refusal names each stale record by handle with the paths that differ for that record — so no recording lands the edits of a draft against content other than the content that draft was opened against (owyntkvw). When every base matches, the recording proceeds exactly as it otherwise would; this decision adds a refusal where a base and the owned set disagree, and adds nothing to a recording that is not refused (rvyrosmp).

The base is written once and kept. Landing takes none of the registry's documents away — a landed record is retained rather than deleted — so the base is not cleared from the record when its draft lands, and a landed record still carries the content its draft was opened against (twpvqstu). The refusal guards only the recording that would land that draft: once that recording has happened there is no recording left for the base to guard, and the base stays in the record as what the draft was opened against (szvotxpq, rvyrosmp). The comparison never rewrites it: each recording compares the base as the opening wrote it against the owned set as it stands then, so a stale record stays stale unless something other than a recording changes it, and nothing here says what that something is (twpvqstu).

Deliberately not here. The encoding of a content identity — the algorithm, length and textual form of the value, and whether the base is one field holding an entry per path or one field per path — is not fixed; only that the base is a value per owned path determined by that path's content (twpvqstu). The refusal's exact wording, separators, ordering, stream and exit status are not fixed, only that it names the handle and the differing paths; neither is whether the comparison is made eagerly or one path at a time, nor exactly where between answering the argument surface and writing anything the read is taken (rvyrosmp). What a stale draft may then do — be re-based, be redrafted, be abandoned, be removed — belongs to a commitment about repair rather than to this one, and nothing here decides it. Concurrent writers and any locking, how a handle is generated, and the record's other fields and their lifetime beyond the opening writing `open` and the landing being the recording, are each settled elsewhere and can change without touching what is settled here: a base of the owned set written into the record at opening, compared against the owned set at landing, and a refusal that names the differing paths (twpvqstu, szvotxpq, owyntkvw, rvyrosmp).
content.rationale:
This node cashes a deferral the record's own parent made: a draft's record is keyed by a handle and carries its node, edit and workspace as references, and its base content, with its state and lifetime, is left to a separate commitment (owyntkvw). The base is that commitment, written so that nothing the parent settled has to move. Identity stays the handle, because a key is what picks one record out and every candidate for the base fails that test: two records may carry equal bases, no entry names a node, an edit or a workspace, and no entry could stand where `.deccy/work/<handle>.json` puts the record (owyntkvw, twpvqstu). The three references stay three, because the base names no part of a draft; calling it a reference would be false, and the record already carries a field of the same third kind, the state the opening writes as `open` (szvotxpq). Read as scoping identity rather than closing the field set, the parent's sentence is untouched; read as closing it, nothing here would survive, so the reading is stated in the decision itself rather than left to the reader.

The base is a content identity rather than a change id because a draft must catch a change to the owned content, and a change's own identity does not move when its content does; a change id would also be an attribution the registry does not have, since a record is not attributed to a change at all (owyntkvw). Taking it at opening is forced by the opening's own shape: the record first exists then, the workspace the draft is written in is created then, and any later base would describe content the caller never saw (szvotxpq). Its extent is the owned set as the ownership rule defines it — the node document, plus the ref paths when `ref` is an array, the node document alone when inline — because a base over the working copy's tree, the change's whole tree or paths the node does not own would attribute to the node content it does not own (xzxtxymq). Both reads cross the jj seam at the owning change under the caller-supplied binary and root, for the reason the single-document read exists at all: the working copy materialises only what sits at its own revision, so a base or a comparison taken from it would describe content that is not the node's at the change it is read at (nqktpzuu). The refusal is placed at the recording because recording is what landing is: `record <path>... --to <id>` is the only thing that moves edits into a change, so a refusal there lands nothing, needs no second verb, creates no node, and leaves `--to` naming the one change the edits would have entered; the refusal refuses placement instead of redirecting it (rvyrosmp).

Naming the differing paths, and comparing the whole owned set rather than the paths the call names, is what makes the refusal usable: the caller learns which owned content moved, and a recording that names one path is refused when another owned path has moved, because the node's document and its refs stand together and an edit made against content the node no longer owns is exactly what must not land. With several records naming one node the bases are several, so each record's base governs the same recording and the refusal names each stale record by handle: a recording is refused if any draft it could land was opened against content that has since moved (owyntkvw). The base is kept rather than cleared at landing because the registry retains a landed record as it was and a comparison does not rewrite the document (twpvqstu); the guard simply has no recording left to stand in front of.

What is left out is left out for a reason: the encoding, the exact refusal text and exit status, the timing of the read, and what repair a stale draft may have are each changeable without touching the three clauses that matter — a base of the owned set written at opening, a comparison against the owned set at landing, and a refusal that names the differing paths. Fixing any of them here would make this commitment answer questions no prerequisite asks and freeze details a reader cannot check against the record.
